findings.why: The project's changelog rule keys on user-facing change, and there is none here by the phase's own construction. Prescribing the artifact anyway adds a review surface (and a wrong statement in a shipped file) without reducing any risk — the second shape of over-specification. It also mildly contradicts the phase's own acceptance criteria, which is the sort of internal tension that costs the implementing agent time to resolve.
findings.recommendation: Either drop step 6 and its AC from this phase and let phase 7's step 8 carry the single accurate entry, or keep it but specify the wording so it is true at land time (e.g. 'adds the mechanism for removing workflow files superseded by a rename; no files are superseded yet').

findings.concern: Step 1 prescribes SHA-256 fingerprints as the representation of known previously-emitted content, a mechanism the implementer could reasonably choose differently
findings.location: phase-6 Step 1 ('the set of known content fingerprints (SHA-256 of each previously-emitted body)') and AC 1
findings.what_fails: The constraint that actually matters — stated well in the Safety constraints section — is 'confirm the content matches one of the known previously-emitted bodies for that engine; anything else is skipped and reported.' Step 1 goes further and fixes the representation to a set of SHA-256 digests. Equally safe alternatives exist (embedding the prior bodies as `include_str!` constants alongside the current ones, which is exactly how `generate_workflows` already sources its content and would keep the table's provenance auditable by `diff`), and the choice cannot be validated in this phase at all, since the table ships empty and the first real fingerprints are captured in phase 7.
findings.why: This is the first shape of over-specification: an implementation decision safely left to whoever carries it out. It also quietly encodes an ongoing maintenance obligation (someone must remember to add a digest on every future template edit) as a plan-level fiat rather than as a property the implementer weighs against alternatives. The plan's own justification in step 1 argues only against name-only and current-bytes-only matching — it does not argue for hashes over stored bytes.
findings.recommendation: State the requirement, not the encoding: each superseded entry pairs a previously-emitted name with an identification of every previously-emitted body for that engine, sufficient to distinguish a pristine prior emission from a user-modified file. Note the pre- and post-phase-4 template bytes as the first two entries phase 7 must capture, and leave digest-vs-embedded-bytes to the implementer.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: phase-6-cleanup-superseded-emitted-workflows — § Decision/Layering, Steps 2-3, Acceptance Criteria 3 and 6
findings.what_fails: The plan assigns the unlink to two different crates. § Layering says core "returns a structured per-file outcome (removed / skipped-because-modified / absent / failed)" while "`rdm-cli` is reduced to calling it, performing the unlink, and printing one line per outcome", and Step 3 repeats that the CLI performs the unlink. But AC3 requires "the core function reports it removed — unit test" and AC6 requires "A failed removal (e.g. permissions) reports and does not fail the emit — unit test", and Step 2 lists a "failed-removal branch" among the core branches under test. If the CLI performs the unlink, core cannot observe or report `removed` or `failed`, and neither AC3 nor AC6 is satisfiable as a rdm-core unit test.
findings.why: An implementer who follows § Layering/Step 3 literally builds a pure-decision core function, then finds two acceptance criteria unreachable and either relocates the tests (silently weakening AC6, the permission-failure guarantee) or refactors mid-phase. Both branches produce a different verification surface than the one the ACs promise.
findings.recommendation: Pick one and say it in both places. The AC set implies core should perform the unlink and return the outcome (including the `Err` -> `failed` mapping), with `rdm-cli` reduced to printing one line per outcome — which also keeps the safety-critical path under core's matchable errors as § Layering argues. Alternatively keep the unlink in the CLI, rename core's outcomes to intents (`remove` / `skip-modified` / `absent`), and re-scope AC3/AC6 to CLI-level tests.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: phase-6-cleanup-superseded-emitted-workflows — Step 1 ("The first fingerprints come from the pre- and post-phase-4 template bytes")
findings.what_fails: Step 1 scopes the known-fingerprint set to two bodies per engine (pre- and post-phase-4 template bytes), but the emitted bodies have many more historical versions: `git log --follow` over `rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/autopilot.js` yields 14 commits and 14 distinct blob hashes (13 for the local `.claude/workflows/autopilot.js`). A downstream repo that ran `agent-config claude --skills --out <dir>` at any other point matches no fingerprint and is classified skipped-because-modified.
findings.why: The mechanism then no-ops for most real upgrade paths, and the stale `autopilot.js` beside `rdm-wf-autopilot.js` — the exact duplicate-listing hazard this phase exists to prevent before phase 7 — survives for those users, degraded to a report line. This is the same failure mode Step 1 itself argues against for the current-bytes-only comparison, just moved from one version to two.
findings.recommendation: State the population policy explicitly: phase 7 captures a fingerprint for every previously *released* emitted body of each engine (enumerable from the template files' git history), not just the phase-4 boundary pair — or, if partial coverage plus a skip report is the accepted outcome, say so here so phase 7 does not inherit an unstated completeness expectation.

findings.concern: restraint
findings.location: phase-6-cleanup-superseded-emitted-workflows — Step 1 ("SHA-256 of each previously-emitted body") and Step 2 ("takes ... the table as an argument")
findings.what_fails: For a phase whose shipped behavior is a deliberate no-op (empty table), the plan pins both the digest algorithm and the dependency-injection signature. SHA-256 is not a free choice: rdm-core's dependencies are serde, serde_yaml, chrono, toml, nucleo-matcher, serde_json — none hashing — so it forces a new crate (plus a `cargo deny` pass) or hand-rolled code, and std's `DefaultHasher` is documented as unstable across releases so it is not a substitute. None of that is acknowledged in the plan.
findings.why: Both decisions are implementation detail that the implementer (or phase 7, which actually captures the bytes and knows how many it must cover) is better placed to make; specifying them here adds surface to review without reducing risk, and the unmentioned dependency implication means the constraint is being imposed without its cost being weighed.
findings.recommendation: Specify the requirement — "a file is removed only when its content matches a known previously-emitted body of that engine" and "the table must be injectable so unit tests can drive a synthetic non-empty one" — and leave the digest/representation to the implementer. If SHA-256 is genuinely required, note that it adds a rdm-core dependency so that cost is decided rather than discovered.

findings.concern: The superseded table is required to be "paired with phase 4 step 8's canonical engine-name table", but phase 4 has no step 8 and explicitly forbids touching `agent_config.rs`; that table is now created by phase 7, which cannot start until phase 6 lands.
findings.location: phase-6-cleanup-superseded-emitted-workflows — Steps §1 ("paired with phase 4 step 8's canonical engine-name table") and AC #1 ("paired with phase 4's canonical engine-name table")
findings.what_fails: Phase 4's body states: "**Engine-name single-sourcing is NOT in this phase** — it moved to phase 7 (`split-step-8-engine-name-single-sourcing`, resolved 2026-07-25) … **This phase does not open `agent_config.rs` at all.**", and phase 4 carries an explicit "**NEGATIVE criterion:** `rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs` is untouched". Phase 7 step 4 is what pairs each `include_str!` with its `relative_path` in ONE table entry per engine — and phase 7's context says "**Depends on phase 6. Do not start before it has landed.**" So phase 6's step 1 and AC #1 reference an artifact that provably does not exist when phase 6 runs and cannot exist until after it, a circular ordering. Today `generate_workflows()` (rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs:351-364) is three inline `WorkflowFile` literals with no name table at all. AC #1 is therefore unsatisfiable as written.
findings.why: An implementer following the plan literally either stalls on an unmeetable acceptance criterion, or invents the canonical engine-name table themselves — performing phase 7 step 4's single-sourcing refactor inside phase 6, which phase 7 deliberately sequenced after the rename ("the rename is the forcing function and the true site inventory can be taken as input rather than assumed") and which phase 4 deliberately declined. That is a scope decision the roadmap has already settled in the opposite direction, so the plan as written drives the wrong build.
findings.recommendation: Drop the pairing requirement from step 1 and AC #1. State instead that phase 6 lands a standalone (empty) superseded table keyed by the emitted `relative_path` values as they exist today, and that phase 7 step 4 folds it into the canonical engine-name entry when it collapses `include_str!`/`relative_path` into one entry per engine. If the pairing must be asserted somewhere, move that AC to phase 7.

findings.concern: The layering decision (core decides, CLI unlinks) contradicts the outcome vocabulary and the acceptance criteria, which require the *core* function to report files as `removed` / `failed` and to be unit-tested on those branches.
findings.location: phase-6-cleanup-superseded-emitted-workflows — Decision §Layering, Steps §2-3 and §5, AC #3 and AC #6
findings.what_fails: The Decision section assigns the unlink to the CLI: "`rdm-cli` is reduced to calling it, performing the unlink, and printing one line per outcome", and step 3 repeats it ("call the core function after writing, perform the unlink"). But the same Decision section says core "returns a structured per-file outcome (removed / skipped-because-modified / absent / failed)", AC #3 says "the core function reports it removed", AC #6 requires "A failed removal (e.g. permissions) reports and does not fail the emit … — unit test", and step 5 puts planted-mutation self-tests on "the `rdm-core` unit tests driving the synthetic non-empty table … the remove / skip-because-modified / failed-removal branches". A function that never calls `fs::remove_file` cannot observe that a removal succeeded or failed with EPERM, so those branches cannot exist in core and cannot be exercised by a `rdm-core` unit test.
findings.why: The implementer must resolve the contradiction one of two ways — move the unlink into core (contradicting the Decision section and the `anyhow`-vs-matchable-errors rationale), or keep it in the CLI and relocate the failed-removal test to `rdm-cli/tests/cli_agent_config.rs` (contradicting AC #3/#6/step 5). Either resolution still produces working cleanup, so this is an implementation-note defect rather than a wrong goal, but it makes at least one acceptance criterion unverifiable as literally stated.
findings.recommendation: Pick one split and state it consistently. The cleanest fit with the stated layering: core returns a decision vocabulary of `remove` / `skip-modified` / `absent` (no `removed`/`failed`), unit-tested in `rdm-core` against the synthetic table; the CLI performs the unlink, converts an unlink error into a reported-but-non-fatal `failed` line, and that branch is covered by a `rdm-cli` test. Reword AC #3 and AC #6 to name the layer that actually owns each branch.

findings.concern: The fingerprint set the plan specifies ("the pre- and post-phase-4 template bytes") covers two snapshots, while the shipped workflow templates have many distinct released versions — so for most upgrading downstream repos the cleanup will skip-and-report rather than remove, leaving the ambiguity phase 7 exists to eliminate.
findings.location: phase-6-cleanup-superseded-emitted-workflows — Steps §1 ("The first fingerprints come from the pre- and post-phase-4 template bytes")
findings.what_fails: `git log --follow` shows 14 / 27 / 19 distinct committed versions of `rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/{autopilot,dispatch-phase,review-refute-fix}.js` respectively (the templates are the byte-identical `include_str!` of the frequently-edited `.claude/workflows/*.js`). Any downstream repo that ran `agent-config claude --skills --out <dir>` against a version other than the two captured snapshots holds an `autopilot.js` matching no known fingerprint, so — per the stated safety rule "Content matching no known fingerprint is skipped-and-reported, never removed" — the stale file survives the re-emit and the listing still shows two indistinguishable entries per engine.
findings.why: The phase's stated purpose is that a downstream re-emit after phase 7 is not "strictly worse off". With only two fingerprints, that guarantee holds only for users who last emitted at one of two exact commits. The skip-report is a real mitigation (the user is told), but the plan should say so explicitly rather than implying the cleanup is generally effective, and it should say which versions matter.
findings.recommendation: Clarify in step 1 that the fingerprint list is the bytes of every *released* version of each template emitted under the superseded name (enumerable from git history at phase 7 time), not just two snapshots — or, if two is a deliberate cost/benefit call, say so and state the residual: users on other versions get a skip-and-report line telling them to remove the file manually. Either way phase 7's CHANGELOG entry (its step 8) should not claim "no manual `rm` is required" unconditionally.

findings.concern: Step 1 anchors this phase's mechanism to a 'canonical engine-name table introduced by phase 4 step 8' that phase 4 explicitly no longer creates — and phase 7, which does own it, is blocked on this phase landing first
findings.location: Steps, step 1 ("paired with the canonical engine-name table introduced by phase 4 step 8") and Acceptance Criterion 1 ("paired with phase 4's canonical engine-name table")
findings.what_fails: `rdm phase show 4 --roadmap project-agnostic-lane` states: "**Engine-name single-sourcing is NOT in this phase** — it moved to phase 7 (`split-step-8-engine-name-single-sourcing`, resolved 2026-07-25)... **This phase does not open `agent_config.rs` at all.**" and carries an explicit NEGATIVE acceptance criterion: "`rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs` is untouched — engine-name single-sourcing belongs to phase 7". Phase 7's body then says "**Depends on phase 6. Do not start before it has landed.**" So the artifact step 1 pairs against is created by a phase that cannot start until this one lands. There is no canonical engine-name table in the tree today either: `rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs:351` `generate_workflows()` is a hand-written `vec![]` of three `WorkflowFile` literals with inline `relative_path` strings and no name table. AC1 as written is unsatisfiable at this phase's completion, and an implementing agent that tries to satisfy it by creating the canonical table here silently absorbs phase 7's step 4 scope (the ~150 engine-name literals across `verify-workflow-*.sh`) that phase 7's body deliberately deferred to itself.
findings.why: This is not a stylistic ordering preference: phase 4 states the prohibition as a negative AC and phase 7 states the dependency direction as a hard one, so the plan as written contradicts two stated constraints of its own roadmap and creates a circular dependency (6 needs 7's table; 7 must not start before 6).
findings.recommendation: Drop the pairing from step 1 and AC1. Specify the superseded-name table as free-standing in this phase — e.g. a `SUPERSEDED_WORKFLOW_NAMES: &[(&str, &[&str])]` keyed by the current `relative_path` literals already present in `generate_workflows()`, empty at landing — and state that phase 7 is responsible for folding it into the canonical engine-name table it introduces, at the same time it populates the entries. That preserves the 6-before-7 order this phase's Context depends on without asserting a prerequisite that does not and cannot exist yet.

findings.concern: The safety constraint 'confirm the file's content matches a known previously-emitted version' has no defined source of previously-emitted content, and the only content rdm carries is the current `include_str!` bytes — which phases 1–4 of this same roadmap rewrite
findings.location: Safety constraints, bullet 3 ("Only remove a file rdm plausibly wrote"); Steps, step 1 (the table holds names only); Acceptance Criterion 3
findings.what_fails: `generate_workflows()` embeds exactly one version of each script (`include_str!("templates/workflows/autopilot.js")` etc., `rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs:351-366`); nothing in the crate stores prior emitted bytes or their hashes, and step 1's table is specified as names only. Phases 1, 2, 3 and 4 of this roadmap all rewrite the bodies of those same three shipped scripts (phase 4's ACs require `grep -c 'target/debug/rdm'` to return ZERO in each `rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/*.js`). So by the time phase 7 populates the table, a downstream repo's stale `autopilot.js` — emitted from any earlier rdm release — will not byte-match the then-current content, the file gets classified as user-modified, and the cleanup skips it. The exact population this phase exists to protect (users who already ran `agent-config --skills --out <dir>` before the rename) keeps both `autopilot.js` and `rdm-wf-autopilot.js` in the listing, which the Context paragraph identifies as "strictly worse off than before".
findings.why: The alternative reading — embed a growing set of historical script bytes or hashes in the crate — pulls against the single-source byte-identity model CLAUDE.md states for this surface (templates are "byte-identical to this repo's own `.claude/workflows/` copies", gated by `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh`), and would need a maintenance rule for when a version enters the set that no step defines. Either way the phase ships a mechanism whose primary acceptance criterion cannot be met by real upgraders, so the approach is underspecified at the point that decides whether it works.
findings.recommendation: Pick and state the provenance rule explicitly in step 1. The cheapest version that survives content churn: store a set of SHA-256 digests per superseded name (`&[(&str, &[&str /* digests */])]`), seed it in phase 7 from the digests of the shipped scripts at each released version, and add a release-time step that appends the outgoing digest. If that maintenance cost is unacceptable, say so and narrow the constraint honestly — e.g. remove only when the stale file's content matches the *currently* emitted content of its renamed counterpart, and document in the CHANGELOG that a file emitted by an older rdm is reported as skipped rather than removed. Either is defensible; leaving it as "a known previously-emitted version" is not implementable as written.

findings.concern: The phase locates the write path in `rdm-core` under a function name that does not exist; the actual loop lives in `rdm-cli`, so following the plan literally puts destructive file-removal logic in the porcelain layer
findings.location: Context, paragraph 2 ("`write_workflows` in `rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs`, plus `rdm-cli`'s `--out` wiring"); Steps, step 2
findings.what_fails: There is no `write_workflows` symbol in the tree — `grep -rn 'write_workflows' --include=*.rs .` matches only two test names in `rdm-cli/tests/cli_agent_config.rs:482,500`. `rdm-core` only *generates* content (`generate_workflows()` returns `Vec<WorkflowFile>`); the write loop is `for workflow in agent_config::generate_workflows() { ... write_output(&path, ...) }` inside `write_skills` at `rdm-cli/src/commands/agent_config.rs:131-138`, joining `base_dir/.claude/workflows`. Step 2 says "extend the write path", which resolves to that CLI function, so an implementer will land unlink-a-user's-file logic in CLI porcelain where `rdm-server`/MCP cannot reach it and where the hand-written-error-enum convention does not apply.
findings.why: CLAUDE.md's architecture section states "Core is the source of truth. CLI and server are thin layers. New interfaces (TUI, MCP server) should call core, not duplicate logic", and splits error handling (`rdm-core`: matchable enums, no `anyhow`; `rdm-cli`: `anyhow` + `.context()`). Cleanup policy — which names are superseded, whether a given file is safe to unlink — is core decision logic, not porcelain.
findings.recommendation: Say explicitly where each half lands: the superseded table and the decide-and-remove function in `rdm-core::agent_config` (returning a report value such as `Vec<CleanupOutcome { path, action: Removed | SkippedModified | Failed(reason) }>`, with a `# Errors` doc section per the missing_docs rule), and `rdm-cli` reduced to calling it and printing the report per step 3. Also correct the Context paragraph — it should name `generate_workflows()` in `rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs:351` and the write loop in `rdm-cli/src/commands/agent_config.rs:131`, so the implementing agent does not start by searching for a function that isn't there.

findings.concern: The core/CLI split is specified down to a four-variant outcome taxonomy that contradicts the division of labor the same plan mandates
findings.location: Decision § "Layering" ("returns a structured per-file outcome (removed / skipped-because-modified / absent / failed)") vs. Step 3 ("Have `rdm-cli`'s emit loop call the core function after writing, perform the unlink") and AC "A failed removal (e.g. permissions) reports and does not fail the emit ... — unit test"
findings.what_fails: If `rdm-cli` performs the unlink, `rdm-core`'s function never attempts a removal and cannot observe or return a `failed` outcome — the failure occurs in the CLI, after core has already returned. The AC then demands a *unit test* (in the crate the plan places the decision in) for a branch that crate structurally cannot reach. An implementer must either move the unlink into core (contradicting step 3) or downgrade the AC to a CLI-level test (contradicting the AC's "unit test" and the Layering rationale). The `absent` variant is similarly surface-only: the plan gives it no reporting behavior — step 3 prints "a line per removed file and a distinct line per skipped-because-modified file", so `absent` is a variant with no consumer.
findings.why: "Core decides, CLI reports" is the actual constraint and is well justified by CLAUDE.md's layering rule. Enumerating the exact variant set on top of it was detail past the point of reducing risk: it added a decision the plan got wrong, and the wrongness propagates into a non-negotiable acceptance criterion. This is restraint shape (2) — the extra specificity created new surface (an unsatisfiable AC) rather than removing risk.
findings.recommendation: State the constraint and stop: `rdm-core` owns the match/skip decision and the superseded table; `rdm-cli` performs the unlink and prints one line per outcome. Drop the enumerated variant list from the plan and let the implementer choose the shape. Reword the failed-removal AC to be surface-agnostic ("a failed unlink reports and does not fail the emit — covered by a test") so it can be satisfied wherever the unlink actually lives.

findings.concern: Step 4 mandates a new shell-harness section that the plan itself says can only assert non-events, duplicating an emptiness assertion already required in Rust
findings.location: Step 4 ("the shipped table is empty, so no end-to-end removal is reachable ... Also assert the shipped table is empty") plus AC 1 ("its SHIPPED contents are EMPTY at this phase's completion — asserted by a test") and AC 2 ("With an empty table, `agent-config` removes nothing — asserted by a test")
findings.what_fails: The same compile-time fact — the shipped table is empty — is asserted three times across two harnesses (a Rust emptiness test, a Rust empty-table-no-op test, and a shell assertion). The remaining shell assertions ("an unrelated user-authored file survives re-emission", "an emitted-name file is rewritten rather than removed") are indistinguishable from the pre-phase behavior where no cleanup code exists at all, so the new `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` section passes vacuously by construction and cannot be made non-vacuous at this phase — which is why step 5 has to route the planted-mutation proof through the Rust tests instead.
findings.why: Restraint shape (2): each added assertion is itself surface that must be written, reviewed, and maintained across a rename that phase 7 will touch again. A shell section that provably cannot fail at this phase buys no risk reduction over the Rust coverage that already exists, and the phase's own "Verification split" paragraph concedes the meaningful end-to-end assertion belongs in phase 7.
findings.recommendation: Keep exactly one emptiness assertion (the Rust one) and defer the new `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` section to phase 7, where the table is populated and the section can actually fail. If a shell touchpoint is wanted here, limit it to extending the existing Pi/`--user` negative for the "creates no `.claude/workflows`" constraint, which is real behavior at this phase.

findings.concern: Step 1 pins the fingerprint mechanism to SHA-256 specifically, committing `rdm-core` to a hashing dependency it does not currently have
findings.location: Step 1: "the set of known content fingerprints (SHA-256 of each previously-emitted body)"
findings.what_fails: `rdm-core/Cargo.toml` lists serde, serde_yaml, chrono, toml, nucleo-matcher, serde_json — no hashing crate. Taking "SHA-256" literally means adding `sha2` (and a `cargo deny` surface) purely to compare a handful of embedded strings, or hand-rolling a digest. The plan's own justification only requires *some* stable identity for previously-emitted bodies; nothing about the safety argument depends on the digest being SHA-256, or on it being a digest at all.
findings.why: Restraint shape (1): the algorithm choice is an implementation decision that can safely be left to whoever carries it out, and fixing it in the plan forecloses cheaper options (embedded literal bodies compared directly, a short non-cryptographic hash, a length+hash pair) without the plan having weighed the dependency cost.
findings.recommendation: Relax the wording to "a stable content fingerprint of each previously-emitted body (digest or embedded bytes — implementer's choice, no new dependency if avoidable)" and keep the binding requirement, which is the one that carries the safety argument: content matching no known fingerprint is skipped and reported, never removed.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: Steps step 1; Acceptance Criteria bullet 1 ("paired with phase 4's canonical engine-name table")
findings.what_fails: Step 1 instructs the implementer to add the superseded table "paired with phase 4 step 8's canonical engine-name table", and AC 1 makes that pairing a checkable criterion. Phase 4 has no step 8. Its context says the step-8 rationale "was verifiably false", that engine-name single-sourcing "moved to phase 7 (split-step-8-engine-name-single-sourcing, resolved 2026-07-25)", and "This phase does not open agent_config.rs at all" — reinforced by phase 4's NEGATIVE AC that rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs is untouched. Phase 7 confirms it absorbed the work, and phase 7 lands AFTER phase 6.
findings.why: The anchor this phase's central artifact is supposed to attach to will not exist when phase 6 runs, and by design will not exist until the phase that DEPENDS on phase 6. An implementer following the plan as written has two bad options: go looking for a table that isn't there and stall, or create the canonical engine-name table here — pulling phase 7's explicitly-owned single-sourcing refactor (~150 harness literals, the WORKFLOWS pinned list, agent_config.rs engine names) forward into a phase scoped to cleanup. That is a scope error, and AC 1 cannot be satisfied as written either way.
findings.recommendation: Drop the phase-4 pairing. Restate step 1 and AC 1 as self-contained: the superseded table is keyed by the engine's current emitted relative_path as generate_workflows() already declares it (the literals "autopilot.js", "dispatch-phase.js", "review-refute-fix.js"), with no dependency on a canonical name table. If pairing with the single-sourced table is genuinely wanted, state it as phase 7's job to re-key this table when it introduces that table, and say so in phase 7 rather than asserting the table already exists here.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: Decision § Layering ("rdm-cli is reduced to calling it, performing the unlink") vs Steps step 2 / Acceptance Criteria bullets 3 and 6
findings.what_fails: The Layering decision assigns the unlink to rdm-cli and leaves core with the decision only. But step 2 says the core function "returns a structured per-candidate outcome" whose variants include `removed` and `failed`, AC 3 requires "the core function reports it removed", and AC 6 requires the failed-removal-does-not-fail-the-emit behavior to be covered by a unit test. A function that does not unlink cannot report `removed` or `failed`, and a core unit test cannot exercise a permission failure that happens in the CLI.
findings.why: The two readings put the safety-critical unlink — and the tests proving the failed-removal branch is non-fatal — in different crates. An implementer who follows the Layering paragraph will produce a core function returning `remove` / `skip` intents and then find AC 3 and AC 6 unsatisfiable in rdm-core, or will silently move the unlink into core and contradict the stated layering. Either way one of the phase's own acceptance criteria is failed on a technicality, and the failed-removal test — one of the two safety guarantees this phase exists to establish — is where the ambiguity bites.
findings.recommendation: Pick one and say it. The simpler resolution given the ACs: let the core function perform the unlink itself (it already takes the output directory and does the fs reads for fingerprinting) and return the per-candidate outcome enum including `Removed`/`Failed`; rdm-cli's only job is printing one line per outcome. Then update the Layering paragraph to drop "performing the unlink" from the CLI's responsibilities.

findings.concern: restraint
findings.location: Steps step 1 ("the set of known content fingerprints (SHA-256 of each previously-emitted body)")
findings.what_fails: The plan fixes the digest algorithm at SHA-256. The workspace has no hashing crate today (no sha2/digest/blake3 in any Cargo.toml), so this silently mandates a new dependency, and it forecloses the simpler alternative the safety constraint actually needs: comparing against the previously-emitted bodies directly, or any content-equality scheme.
findings.why: The safety property the phase cares about is "content matches a known previously-emitted version, else skip-and-report". Which comparison mechanism delivers that is an implementation decision that the person carrying it out can make correctly with the constraint alone, and they will be better placed to weigh a new crate dependency against embedding the handful of superseded bodies. Naming the algorithm in the plan adds a decision to review without reducing risk — and because the table ships empty here, no fingerprint value is even produced in this phase.
findings.recommendation: Restate the requirement as the property: each superseded entry carries a previously-emitted name plus enough information to recognize the exact bodies rdm emitted under it; content matching none of them is skipped and reported. Leave the representation (content hash of any algorithm, or the bodies themselves) to the implementer, and note that a new hashing dependency is acceptable but not required.

findings.concern: architectural-fit
findings.location: Steps step 6 / Acceptance Criteria final bullet ("CHANGELOG.md entry under [Unreleased] describing the new cleanup behavior of rdm agent-config — user-facing, so it ships in this commit")
findings.what_fails: With the shipped table empty at this phase's completion — asserted by AC 1 and AC 2 — `rdm agent-config` removes nothing and behaves identically to before. The step nonetheless requires an entry describing "the new cleanup behavior" and justifies it as user-facing. CLAUDE.md's changelog rule triggers on a user-facing change and asks that entries "describe the change from a user's perspective (what they can now do, what was fixed) rather than internal implementation details"; an entry announcing cleanup that cannot occur inverts that.
findings.why: A reader of the [Unreleased] section would conclude that re-running agent-config now cleans up stale emitted workflow files, which is false until phase 7 populates the table. That is worse than no entry: it is the kind of claim the safety-conscious framing of this phase is otherwise careful to avoid, and it invites a downstream user to skip a manual cleanup on the strength of a promise the binary does not keep.
findings.recommendation: Either drop the changelog requirement from this phase and move it to phase 7, where the behavior becomes observable, or keep it here but specify the wording as forward-looking and accurate — e.g. that agent-config now has a cleanup mechanism for files it previously emitted under superseded names, with no names currently listed. Adjust the AC to match whichever is chosen.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: Decisions § "The seven new names are exactly" / "All seven move in one commit"; Files-to-change table, Engines (7) row
findings.what_fails: There are EIGHT engines under `.claude/workflows/`, not seven: `spike-agent-type.js` exists and surfaces in the slash-command/skill listing (it appears in this session's listing as `spike-agent-type: Feasibility spike…`). The plan never mentions it — not in the name list, not in the table, not in the `N=` grep alternation, not in any acceptance criterion. After the phase lands, the listing still contains one bare-named engine.
findings.why: The plan's own stated justification for atomicity is the inference rule: "A prefix scheme applied to a subset is worse than none, because a reader can no longer infer from the *absence* of a prefix whether a listing entry is a skill or an engine." A surviving bare `spike-agent-type` defeats exactly that rule, so the phase's goal is only partially reached. This is not a relitigation of the settled seven names — the engine is simply absent from the inventory. It is also not a transient artifact: it is retained and referenced by path in `docs/workflow-schemas.md:178,223`, `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh:563,566,680,709,713,724,728`, `scripts/verify-workflow-dispatch.sh:2417,2419,2451`, and `docs/mechanical-agent-inventory.md:21`, so nothing else removes it. No acceptance criterion would catch it either — the AC's "fresh run of all seven targeted greps" uses an `N=` alternation that excludes the name.
findings.recommendation: Decide `spike-agent-type` explicitly and record the decision in the plan: either (a) include it as an eighth rename (`rdm-wf-spike-agent-type`, updating its `meta.name` and the ~12 by-path exclusions in the two harnesses and two docs), or (b) delete it if the spike is spent, or (c) state in Decisions why a non-front-door spike artifact is exempt. If (b) or (c), also drop or qualify the "absence of a prefix implies skill" rationale, since it will not hold. Consider adding a gate asserting every `.claude/workflows/*.js` is `rdm-wf-*` so the convention cannot silently regress.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: Reference surface § trailing note: "Lines 157/163 sit inside the `rdm:review-spec` region (98-257), but that local copy is hand-maintained: `gen-skill-review.sh` only gates the shipped templates"; Steps 6; AC "gen-skill-review.sh --check (both modes) pass"

The two engine references the note calls hand-maintained (`main`: `rdm-review/SKILL.md:166,172`) are generated from `lib/review.mjs`'s `find-refute-verdict:local-code-override` block (`main`: review.mjs:535-612, `//|` prose at 537 and 543, both naming `review-refute-fix`). findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria § "The rendered slash-command / skill listing shows the prefixed engine names — **verified by observing the listing, not merely the files**"
findings.what_fails: The plan gives no mechanism for satisfying this AC, and the implementing agent cannot: the skill/slash-command listing is materialized into the session at start, so a rename performed mid-session does not re-render it. This repo's own CLAUDE.md documents the analogous caveat for the sibling registry — "Claude Code watches `.claude/agents/`, but the watcher covers only directories that existed at session start". Every other AC in the plan names a concrete command or grep; this one names an observation with no owner and no command.
findings.why: An AC that cannot be executed within the run either blocks completion or is rubber-stamped, and it is the only AC covering the phase's actual user-visible goal. It is also the one check that would have caught a missed `meta.name` independently of the file-level greps, so leaving it unexecutable removes the intended backstop rather than merely adding ceremony.
findings.recommendation: Split it: keep a mechanical in-run check (each `.claude/workflows/rdm-wf-*.js` filename stem equals its `export const meta.name`, and no `.claude/workflows/*.js` lacks the prefix — this is already half-covered by the second AC), and restate the listing observation as an explicit post-restart confirmation step owned by the human landing the phase, or by a follow-up note, rather than as a criterion the implementing run must tick.

findings.concern: restraint
findings.location: Reference forms 5 and 6; Files-to-change table, Rust wiring and Docs rows; trailing `rdm-review/SKILL.md` note; Steps 6
findings.what_fails: The plan pins exact line numbers throughout (`rdm-review/SKILL.md:43,157,163`, region `98-257`, `README.md:93`, `CLAUDE.md:176`, `docs/workflow-schemas.md:9`, `docs/escalation-protocol.md:117`, `cli_agent_config.rs:415,449-451,474`, `gen-workflow-*.sh:37-39`, `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh:74`). Four of them are already wrong on `main` before phases 4 and 6 land: the `Workflow: review-refute-fix` line the plan calls out twice as `:43` is at `:52`, and `157/163` are at `166/172`; the region is `107-350`, not `98-257`. The seven anchored greps already locate every one of these sites by form, which is the plan's stated method ("What is precomputed here is the **method** … not a frozen answer"). Pinned coordinates that the plan predicts will be stale — and four of which are stale today — invite an implementer to trust a stale pointer over the grep, which is precisely the failure mode Step 6 and finding `local-skill-region-wrongly-called-hand-maintained` show playing out.

findings.concern: The plan enumerates seven engines under `.claude/workflows/`, but the directory holds eight `.js` engines — `spike-agent-type.js` is never mentioned, so following the plan as written leaves an unprefixed engine in the listing, which the plan's own rationale declares worse than not prefixing at all
findings.location: project-agnostic-lane/phase-7-prefix-workflow-engines — Decisions § ("All seven move in one commit"), Files-to-change table (Engines (7)), AC 1 and AC 3
findings.what_fails: `ls .claude/workflows/*.js` returns eight files: the seven named plus `spike-agent-type.js`, whose `meta.name` is `'spike-agent-type'` (`.claude/workflows/spike-agent-type.js:46`) and which does surface in this session's slash-command / skill listing ("spike-agent-type: Feasibility spike: does agent() honor opts.agentType and opts.effort…"). The plan never names it, excludes it, or explains why it is not an engine. After the phase lands, the listing reads `rdm-wf-autopilot`, `rdm-wf-backlog`, … and `spike-agent-type` — an unprefixed entry that IS an engine. That is exactly the state the plan's settled decision calls out as the failure mode: "A prefix scheme applied to a subset is worse than none, because a reader can no longer infer from the *absence* of a prefix whether a listing entry is a skill or an engine." No gate catches it either: the grep alternation `N` omits `spike-agent-type`, so AC 7 ("a fresh run of all seven targeted greps returns only intentional prose") passes vacuously, and AC 1/AC 4 are both scoped to the seven named engines. Only AC 3 ("verified by observing the listing") would expose it, and at that point the implementer has no instruction for what to do — the seven names are marked "settled, do not relitigate".
findings.why: The phase's goal is that a reader can tell an engine from a front door by looking at the listing. One unprefixed engine defeats that inference for every entry, by the plan's own stated reasoning. The omission is silent rather than a decision: nothing in the body says spike-agent-type is out of scope, is scheduled for deletion, or is not an engine, so the implementer either ships the degraded outcome or has to make a scope call the plan declared foreclosed.
findings.recommendation: State the disposition of `spike-agent-type.js` explicitly in the Decisions section — either (a) include it as an eighth rename (`rdm-wf-spike-agent-type`), adding it to the engine list, the `N` grep alternation, and the AC counts, or (b) delete it as a completed spike whose findings are already recorded in `docs/workflow-schemas.md` § "agentType / effort options spike", or (c) keep it bare with a written rationale for why a spike artifact is exempt. Note that (a) also touches its exclusion lines in `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh` (~563-728) and `scripts/verify-workflow-dispatch.sh` (~2417-2451), which match it by filename, and `docs/mechanical-agent-inventory.md:21`; (b) touches the same lines by removing them.

findings.concern: Step 3 tells the implementer to populate phase 6's superseded table with "the pre-rename bare names", but phase 6's table schema requires a name PLUS a set of SHA-256 content fingerprints per superseded entry, and phase 6 explicitly assigns the pre-/post-phase-4 fingerprint capture to phase 7
findings.location: project-agnostic-lane/phase-7-prefix-workflow-engines — step 3, and the corresponding AC ("Phase 6's superseded-name table is populated for the three shipped engines")
findings.what_fails: Phase 6 step 1 defines each entry as "**both** a previously-emitted name **and** the set of known content fingerprints (SHA-256 of each previously-emitted body)", and states: "The first fingerprints come from the pre- and post-phase-4 template bytes, captured when phase 7 populates the table." Phase 7's step 3 and its AC mention only names. An implementer working step 3 from phase 7's text populates names with, at most, the current template bytes. Phase 6's safety rule is "Content matching no known fingerprint is skipped-and-reported, never removed" — so a downstream user who ran `agent-config claude --skills` before phase 4 landed and re-emits after 4+7 has an `autopilot.js` whose bytes match no recorded fingerprint: it is classified modified, left on disk, and the duplicate-listing-entry state phase 6 exists to prevent persists. Phase 7's end-to-end AC would still pass, because the harness seeds the old file from the post-phase-4 bytes it has to hand.
findings.why: Phase 7 is the sole populator of that table, and phase 4 is explicitly "a sequencing preference, not a hard dependency" here — so both the pre- and post-phase-4 byte sets are conditional and have to be retrieved deliberately (from git history, if phase 4 has landed). Leaving that requirement only in phase 6's body means the most likely real-world upgrade path is the one silently left uncovered, behind green gates.
findings.recommendation: Make step 3 explicit: for each of the three shipped engines, record the superseded name plus SHA-256 fingerprints for **every** previously-emitted body — at minimum the current `rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/<name>.js` bytes and, if phase 4 landed first, the pre-phase-4 bytes recovered from git. Add an AC that the end-to-end removal in `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` is exercised against a stale file seeded from a pre-phase-4 fingerprint, not only from the current bytes, so the multi-fingerprint path is proven non-vacuous.

findings.concern: The plan scopes the rename to seven engines, but `.claude/workflows/` holds an eighth live engine — `spike-agent-type.js` — which surfaces bare in the listing. Leaving it unprefixed defeats the plan's own settled invariant that absence-of-prefix identifies a skill.

After the phase lands as written, the listing shows seven `rdm-wf-*` entries, eleven `rdm-*` skills, and one bare `spike-agent-type` — so a reader who applies the plan's own rule ('absence of a prefix ⇒ it is a skill') misclassifies it. findings.recommendation: Either (a) include `spike-agent-type.js` as an eighth rename to `rdm-wf-spike-agent-type.js` — note this additionally requires updating its by-name gate exclusions at `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh:563,566,709,713,724,728`, `scripts/verify-workflow-dispatch.sh:2417,2419,2451` (§7 inventory gate), `docs/mechanical-agent-inventory.md:21`, `docs/workflow-schemas.md:223`, and `docs/token-baseline.json:554,556,570`; or (b) add an explicit, reasoned carve-out to the Decisions section (e.g. 'the spike engine is a temporary probe scheduled for deletion when the spike closes; it is deliberately left unprefixed') and amend AC 3 to assert the listing shows exactly one bare engine entry, with its name pinned. findings.what_fails: `scripts/mine-refuter-corpus.mjs:82`, `scripts/mine-plan-finder-corpus.mjs:80`, and `scripts/measure-refuter-severity.mjs:101` each declare `const LANE_WORKFLOWS = ['autopilot', 'dispatch-phase', 'plan-review', 'backlog', 'estimate', 'document'];` and pass it as `findWorkflowRunFiles(sessionDirs, { workflowNames: LANE_WORKFLOWS })` (mine-refuter:215, mine-plan-finder:202). `scripts/lib/token-report.mjs:174` turns that into an exact-match `new Set(workflowNames)` filter over each sidecar's `workflowName` — which is the engine's `meta.name`. After step 2 rewrites `meta.name` to `rdm-wf-*`, every future run's sidecar carries the new name, the set match yields zero, and all three instruments silently mine an empty corpus rather than erroring. Their gates do not catch it: `scripts/verify-refuter-agreement.sh`, `scripts/verify-finder-collapse.sh`, and `scripts/verify-token-report.sh` §6 drive committed fixtures under `tests/fixtures/{refuter-agreement,finder-collapse,token-refuter-severity}/` that still hold the old names, so they pass green. Checking each plan grep against `LANE_WORKFLOWS`: form 1/7 need a `.claude/workflows/` or template path (absent), form 2 is scoped to `*.js` engine files only, form 3 needs `workflow(`, form 4 needs a backtick plus adjacent 'Workflow', form 5 needs a line-anchored `Workflow:`, form 6 needs a `.js` suffix. All seven miss it.
findings.why: CLAUDE.md's CI Expectations mandate `for f in scripts/verify-*.sh; do bash "$f"; done` — all 17 harnesses — and separately designate these instruments as load-bearing evidence surfaces ('Run it after touching scripts/lib/token-report.mjs, scripts/measure-lane-tokens.mjs, scripts/measure-refuter-severity.mjs, or either fixture tree'). The plan's harness AC enumerates only the ten `verify-workflow-*` scripts plus the distribution harness — while explicitly warning against relying on the glob — and omits `verify-refuter-agreement.sh`, `verify-finder-collapse.sh`, and `verify-token-report.sh` entirely, along with `scripts/mine-*.mjs` and `scripts/measure-*.mjs` from the file table. The failure is worse than a missed edit because it is a green-gate failure: the phase reports success while the token/refuter/finder measurement lane goes blind on all subsequent runs.
findings.recommendation: Add the runtime-name-as-data-key form as an explicit eighth reference form with its own grep (e.g. `grep -rnE "LANE_WORKFLOWS|workflowNames" scripts`), add `scripts/{mine-refuter-corpus,mine-plan-finder-corpus,measure-refuter-severity}.mjs` to the file table, and decide and record the corpus-continuity policy: whether `LANE_WORKFLOWS` becomes the new names only (abandoning pre-rename sidecars), or the union of old and new names so historical runs stay minable. Extend the harness AC to `verify-refuter-agreement.sh`, `verify-finder-collapse.sh`, and `verify-token-report.sh`, and state whether the committed fixtures keep their pre-rename names (they should — they are historical records).

findings.concern: The plan pins exact line numbers for references it simultaneously predicts will move, and the most detailed of those citations is already wrong against `main` — five of six cited `rdm-review/SKILL.md` lines point at unrelated text, and both `rdm:review-spec` region bounds are off.
findings.location: phase-7-prefix-workflow-engines § 'The reference surface' — reference form 5, form 6, and the `rdm-review/SKILL.md` paragraph following the files table
findings.what_fails: The plan states flatly: "`rdm-review/SKILL.md` carries **six** engine references — lines 22, 36, 40, 43, 157, 163". Checked against `main`: the file does carry exactly six `review-refute-fix` references, but they are at lines 20, 22, 49, 52, 166, 172. Of the six cited numbers only 22 is a real reference. Line 36 is a `git log --oneline -20` orientation step, lines 40 and 43 are bare ``` code fences, line 157 is the word "internals.", line 163 is prose about SAFETY comments. Line 20 — a genuine reference — is not cited at all. Reference form 5 compounds it: "`.claude/skills/rdm-review/SKILL.md:43` is a standalone line reading `Workflow: review-refute-fix`" — line 43 is a code fence; the real standalone line is 52. The `rdm:review-spec` region is cited as "(98-257)"; actual bounds on `main` are 107-337 (and 107-350 on the current branch). The stale-citation pattern is not confined to that file: the plan cites `CLAUDE.md:176` as a form-6 site, but the form-6 hits in `CLAUDE.md` are at 175/180/184/185/188/192 on this branch, and line 176 is blank on `main`. An implementing agent that treats these as the edit list edits code fences and unrelated prose while leaving line 20 stale.
findings.why: This is over-specification, not under-specification. The plan already supplies seven anchored, self-updating greps that locate every one of these sites by form, and it explicitly warns not to work from a bare-word grep — that method is the genuinely valuable precomputation. Layering line numbers on top adds no risk reduction: they cannot be more accurate than the greps, they are demonstrably already wrong, and the plan itself says the surface will move ("phases 4 and 6 land first and will have moved this surface, so a count mismatch against the enumeration below is expected"). Both stated dependencies are still `not-started`, and phase 4's own scope is rewriting `agent_config.rs` and the harnesses — so every remaining accurate citation (`cli_agent_config.rs:415,449-451,474`, `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh:74`, `gen-workflow-{review,estimate}.sh:37-39`) is scheduled to decay before this phase runs. False precision is worse than no precision here, because it invites the implementer to skip the greps.
findings.recommendation: Drop the line-number citations and keep the counts plus the anchored greps. Where a specific site genuinely needs calling out (form 5's standalone `Workflow: review-refute-fix` line, the `rdm:review-spec` region), identify it by quoted anchor text and marker name rather than by line number — e.g. "the standalone line `Workflow: review-refute-fix` in `rdm-review/SKILL.md`" and "the `rdm:review-spec:begin`/`:end` markers". Correct or delete the `rdm-review/SKILL.md` reference tally; as written it is wrong in five of six positions and misses a real reference.

findings.concern: An acceptance criterion asserts that two files outside the change set were not changed, and that negative AC collides with a sibling AC about stale engine names.
findings.location: phase-7-prefix-workflow-engines § Acceptance Criteria — "`verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` names its engines in exactly one place, and the TWO real generator consumer lists each remain a single list. `gen-skill-review.sh` and `mechanical-tier-check.sh` are confirmed to carry no engine-name list and are left untouched" (and the matching bullets in step 4)
findings.what_fails: The second half of that AC is satisfied by doing nothing to two files that appear nowhere in the plan's own files-to-change table. It is also in tension with the sibling AC "A fresh run of all seven targeted greps returns only intentional prose": `scripts/gen-skill-review.sh:45` reads "# Verdict-point-2 span with a recap of the `review-refute-fix` Workflow" — a form-4 backticked-engine-adjacent-to-Workflow match. So "left untouched" and "no stale engine names outside intentional prose" cannot both hold literally; a reviewer checking the ACs must resolve which one governs. (The plan's narrower claim that neither script holds an engine-name *list* is correct, and `mechanical-tier-check.sh` does indeed carry no `.js`/`.mjs` reference.)
findings.why: The load-bearing invariant — "each script names its engines in exactly one place" — is already fully carried by the first half of the AC. Appending a verified-negative on two out-of-scope files converts a research note into a gate, adding review surface without reducing risk, and in this case introduces an internal inconsistency the reviewer now has to adjudicate. The same shape appears in step 4's instruction to "confirm both are clean rather than looking for a list that does not exist", which is useful guidance to the implementer but does not need to be promoted to an acceptance criterion.
findings.recommendation: Cut the "`gen-skill-review.sh` and `mechanical-tier-check.sh` are confirmed to carry no engine-name list and are left untouched" clause from the AC, keeping only the single-place invariant for the files actually being changed. Retain the step-4 note as an implementation aside so the implementer does not go hunting. Separately decide the `gen-skill-review.sh:45` prose reference: either list that file in the step-8 docs/prose sweep, or state it as an explicit carve-out under the stale-names AC.

findings.concern: coherence
findings.location: .claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs:537,543 (rendered into .claude/skills/rdm-review/SKILL.md); plan § "The reference surface" closing note + step 6 + Files table row "Libs (7)"
findings.what_fails: The plan's closing note states: "Lines 157/163 sit inside the `rdm:review-spec` region (98-257), but that local copy is hand-maintained: `gen-skill-review.sh` only gates the shipped templates, none of which reference an engine today." Both halves are false. `scripts/gen-skill-review.sh` has a `--target local` axis that stamps `.claude/skills/{rdm-review,rdm-plan-review}/SKILL.md` (its own header: "local — this repo's own dogfood skill copies … Nothing else re-stamps these, so without this target they drift silently"), and `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh:371,376` runs `--check --target local` in BOTH modes. The two in-region `review-refute-fix` references on main (SKILL.md:166 and :172, not 157/163) are generated from `//|` prose at `lib/review.mjs:537` and `:543`, inside the `find-refute-verdict:local-code-override` block. The Files table compounds this by listing `lib/review.mjs` under "Libs (7) — filenames unchanged, header comments only", when review.mjs must also have its `//|` prose edited.
findings.why: Step 6 asks the implementer to check whether shim prose is inside a stamped region; this note hands them a pre-answered "no" with an authoritative "verified" framing, so the natural action is to hand-edit SKILL.md:166/172 and skip the regenerate. That directly violates CLAUDE.md's stated single-source constraint (the review.mjs skill projection is `--check`-gated; a hand edit breaks the gate). It also means the plan's own acceptance criterion — `gen-skill-review.sh --check` "(both modes)" — omits the `--target local` axis that is the one actually at risk, so the AC as written does not name the check that catches the mistake.
findings.recommendation: Delete or correct the closing note: state that `.claude/skills/rdm-review/SKILL.md`'s in-region engine references ARE generated (via `gen-skill-review.sh --target local --mode code`) from `lib/review.mjs`'s `find-refute-verdict:local-code-override` `//|` block, and must be renamed at the lib, not the SKILL.md. Move `lib/review.mjs` out of the "header comments only" row and note it carries renderable `//|` prose. Extend the generator AC to `gen-skill-review.sh --check` across both `--target shipped` and `--target local` in both modes. Re-verify the exact line numbers at implementation time rather than trusting the cited ones — the six references sit at 22/36/49/52/166/172 on main, not 22/36/40/43/157/163.

findings.concern: restraint
findings.location: plan § step 4 ("Verified inventory") and the two acceptance criteria pinning "exactly one place in `generate_workflows()`" / "names its engines in exactly one place"
findings.what_fails: For a mechanical rename, the plan prescribes the internal data structure of the refactor ("pair each `include_str!` with its `relative_path` in ONE table entry per engine"), pins that shape as a gating acceptance criterion, and freezes ~10 exact line-number citations (`gen-workflow-review.sh:37-39`, `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh:74`, `cli_agent_config.rs:415,449-451,474`, `README.md:93`, `CLAUDE.md:176`, `docs/workflow-schemas.md:9`, `rdm-review/SKILL.md:43,157,163`). Several are already stale against `main` — `CLAUDE.md:176` is a refuter-agreement harness bullet, `README.md:93` is a blank line (the engine names are at :95), and the three `rdm-review/SKILL.md` numbers are off by 3-9 lines — and the plan itself concedes phases 4 and 6 land first and "will have moved this surface."
findings.why: Two of the three ACs about single-sourcing gate on code shape rather than observable behavior, foreclosing a reasonable implementer choice (e.g. a `const` array of `(name, bytes)` tuples) that satisfies the same goal. And detail that is known-stale before work starts is new review surface without risk reduction: the reader must diff every cited line against reality, and the two citations that are actually wrong (F1's note, `CLAUDE.md:176`) are the ones that misled rather than helped. This is a concern, not a gate — the plan's three prior failed dispatch attempts justify most of the precomputation.
findings.recommendation: Keep the anchored grep forms, the front-door collision warning, and the "do NOT add the four unshipped engines" constraint — those are the load-bearing parts. Soften step 4's data-structure prescription to its intent ("each shipped engine's name appears once in `generate_workflows()`; keep the test and doc-test as independent literals") and drop the code-shape ACs in favor of the existing behavioral ones (`generate_workflows_are_byte_identical_to_source`, section 3/4 of the distribution harness). Replace frozen line numbers with the anchored grep that finds them, since the plan already instructs the implementer to re-run the greps.
